issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Add a `Remove` method to `PriorityQueue`
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-collections See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
### Background and motivation When we shipped the `PriorityQueue` class back in .NET 6 we made the explicit decision to not add support for efficient, $\mathcal O(\log n)$ priority updates. This was due to priority updates not being supported without sacrificing overall performance and lack of widespread use in .NET codebases. We have a [separate issue](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/44871) that tracks adding a separate heap type that does support priority updates. Even though the `PriorityQueue` type itself cannot be retrofitted to support efficient priority updates, it can be made to support $\mathcal O(n)$ priority updates. This can be useful in educational contexts or coding interviews, where the actual asymptotic performance is not mission critical and can be overlooked. Put differently, users have asked for this facility so that they can implement Dijkstra's algorithm in leetCode using C#. In the case of the Java, users can encode priority updates in the `PriorityQueue` class by piggybacking on its [built-in remove method](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/PriorityQueue.html#remove-java.lang.Object-). ### API Proposal ```csharp namespace System.Collections.Generic; public partial class PriorityQueue { // Scans the heap for elements equal to the provided value and removes the first occurrence. public bool Remove(TElement element, out TPriority priority, IEqualityComparer? equalityComparer = null); } ``` ### API Usage It's possible to use the above API to encode a $\mathcal O(n)$ priority update as follows: ```C# public static void EnqueueOrUpdate(this PriorityQueue queue, TElement element, TPriority priority) { queue.Remove(element, out _); queue.Enqueue(element, priority); } ``` ### Alternative Designs _No response_ ### Risks It could end up being used in production code. I expect this risk would be mitigated since we're not explicitly adding an "update" API, instead users need to invoke a `Remove` API that will be explicitly documented as a linear-time scan operation.

review_comments:
></remarks> [](http://example.com/codeflow?start=12&length=10)

Can mention the behavior when passing null equalityComparer in the remarks?

>EqualityComparer<TElement>.Default [](http://example.com/codeflow?start=24&length=34)

does using equalityComparer here will prevent the JIT to optimize it? even for value types?
The JIT will devirtualize `EqualityComparer<TElement>.Default.Equals` calls but only when `TElement` is a value type. For reference types it's better to reference the equality comparer from a local.

Since the primary reported purpose of adding this method is to enable non-production scenarios involving implementing Djikstra's algorithm, it'd be good to have a test that does so, to validate that it works, to ensure it's as easy as it should be, and to serve as an example we can point folks to.

How important is the performance of Remove?  If it's really important, we could consider subsequently changing the data storage of PQ, to be two arrays (priorities and elements) rather than one that combines them. Then here this could use IndexOf and get the SIMD benefits where applicable. (Did we try such splitting in the original prototyping/implementation of PQ? In theory it could have benefits even for normal enqueue/dequeue operations, as the priorities we'd be sifting through would be more tightly packed.)

The original prototype did use separate arrays, IIRC we ended up fusing into one to optimize the regular heap operations and enumerator. I don't think the performance of `Remove` is important enough to override the original concerns.

>(TElement element, TPriority priority) = generatedItems[i]; [](http://example.com/codeflow?start=16&length=59)

I think this will be better to make it remove from random index instead of always last one. i.e. use `Random.Next(i)` instead of `i`.

We generally want to avoid nondeterminism in unit tests. I could try using a `Random` instance with a seed, however the `CreatePriorityQueue` already uses pseudorandomness when populating the heap.

Another thing to note is that the index on `generatedItems` is not a predictor of where the element is located within the heap itself, since it is structured based on the priority values.
will be good to add a test inserting same element more than once but with different priority then remove and validate the first match is always removed.
There's no guarantee of what element will get removed in case of duplicates, but you're right that there should some test exercising that particular scenario.
